My mother can help on the second day. I should state my own need clearly, focusing on the part that isn't flexible.
I need the first day off. My son's childcare is closed.
Stated my constraint.

I can work the New Year days if I can have Christmas off.
I have made my proposal and am waiting for a reaction.

I need to make sure they know why it's important to me, especially since I'm the newest. The reunion dinner on the first day is the most important part. I can't miss that. I'll just state my need plainly.
The first day is reunion dinner for my family.
I've stated my most important need. Now I'll wait to see what the others say.

STRATEGY: CHALLENGE. So now Xin Yi has a family reason too. That's three of us who all need the first day off. Marcus has his son, she has the reunion dinner, and I have my family trip. We can't all have it. It's a direct clash.
So all three of us need that first day.
I've pointed out the impasse. Let's see if anyone has a solution.

STRATEGY: CLARIFY. Natalie has summed up the problem well. We're at a stalemate for the first day. I should make it clear that my problem is only the first day. I don't need the second one. Maybe that creates some room for compromise.
I can work the second day. It's just the first one I need.
I have clarified my position to see if it helps resolve the conflict.

STRATEGY: CLARIFY. Marcus's offer to work the second day is helpful. If I work it with him, that day is covered. This simplifies the problem. The main issue now is the first day. Three people want it off, and we need one of them to work with me. I'll state this plainly to move the discussion forward. It shows my proposal helps solve their problem and reminds them what the remaining issue is.
Okay, so if Marcus and I work the second day, that's sorted. We still need one more person for the first day with me.
I've clarified the state of the roster based on Marcus's offer and my proposal. Now it's up to the other three to decide who works the first day.

STRATEGY: DEFEND. Rachel's right. It's now down to me, Natalie, and Marcus for that one spot on the first day. I've already said it's for my family's reunion dinner, and that's not something you can just skip. Marcus has his reason with his son. Natalie hasn't said why. I'm the newest here, and if I give in on something this important, I'll be the one expected to give in every time. I can't work that day.
I cannot work on the first day.
I've made my position clear. Now it's up to the others.

STRATEGY: DEFEND. Xin Yi says she 'cannot' work. Marcus has his childcare issue. Well, my family trip is just as important. I can't be the one to back down just because they sound firm. I need to make it clear my position is just as non-negotiable.
My family's trip starts that day. I also can't work.
I've restated my position firmly. Now it's a clear three-way impasse.

STRATEGY: CLARIFY. Okay, Natalie's reason sounds as fixed as Xin Yi's and mine. We're at a dead end. We all need the first day off, but only one of us can have it. I should point this out to see if anyone has an idea on how to break the stalemate.
So all three of us can't work on the first day. How do we solve this?
Waiting for a response to the impasse.

STRATEGY: DEFEND. They are presenting a situation where my condition for getting Christmas off
    -- that is, that the roster is covered -- can't be met. I need to defend my proposed deal. The core of my defense is that the deal is a package, and it's their collective responsibility to meet the conditions if they want the benefit of me working. My offer isn't charity; it's a trade. It's not my problem to solve their three-way conflict.
That's for you three to figure out. I can work that day, but only if my Christmas leave is approved.
I've made my position clear and put the ball in their court.

Rachel just put the ball back in our court. It's between me, Natalie, and Marcus for that first day. All three of us have said we can't work. My reunion dinner is not something I can miss. Natalie has a trip and Marcus has childcare issues. We're stuck. There is nothing new for me to say. I've made my point, so I'll wait and see what the others suggest.
Waiting to see if Marcus or Natalie will propose a solution or change their position.

STRATEGY: PROPOSE. Okay, so Rachel's making it clear it's on the three of us. We're getting nowhere just repeating that we all need the day off. Since there's no rule, what else is there? A random draw seems like the only fair way to break the tie at this point.
How do we decide then? Draw lots?
I've proposed a way to break the deadlock.

STRATEGY: CHALLENGE. Natalie's suggestion to draw lots feels like a gamble, and I can't afford to lose. My son's care isn't something I can leave to chance. I have to reject this idea and explain why.
I'm not comfortable with that. If I don't get the day off, I have a real problem with childcare.
Waiting for a response to my rejection of the proposal.

Marcus is rejecting the idea of drawing lots. He has a solid reason, childcare. But so do the others, with family trips and reunion dinners. They're at an impasse. My offer to work the New Year days is contingent on one of them working with me, and if they can't decide, my Christmas leave is at risk. This is incredibly frustrating. I've offered a perfectly good solution, and they're the ones who can't agree. It's not my place to decide whose need is greater. They need to sort this out among themselves. I'm just going to wait.
Waiting for them to resolve their conflict over the first CNY day.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Marcus is right to not want to leave it to chance. I feel the same way. My family's reunion dinner isn't something I can gamble on. It's a certainty that I need to be there. I'll agree with him.
I don't want to draw lots either. I can't risk missing my family dinner.
I've agreed with Marcus and restated my non-negotiable position. The problem remains unsolved.

STRATEGY: CHALLENGE. So they've both rejected drawing lots because they can't risk it. Fine. But they haven't suggested anything else. We're still stuck. If a random draw isn't fair, then what is? Someone has to give way, and it's not automatically going to be me. I'll put it back on them.
So if we're not drawing lots, what's the alternative?
I've challenged them to come up with a better solution.

STRATEGY: PROPOSE. Natalie is asking for an alternative, and she's right. Just saying no to drawing lots isn't enough. Our needs are all important to us, so comparing them will probably just cause a fight. Maybe the solution isn't for one of us to give in. We could ask management if there's another option, like getting a temporary staff member for that one day. It's a long shot, but it's a concrete suggestion.
We could ask head office if they can get a temp in for the day. That way we could all take it.
I've proposed an alternative solution.

STRATEGY: ACCEPT. Marcus's idea to get a temp from head office is a good one. It solves the problem of who works the first CNY day, which is the only thing blocking my Christmas leave. If they agree, then my offer stands and I get what I want. I should support this.
That's a good idea. If head office can send someone, that solves the problem.
I've supported the proposal and am waiting to see if the others agree.

STRATEGY: ACCEPT. Marcus's idea to ask for a temp is a good one, and Rachel agrees. This would solve the problem for everyone. I don't have to miss my family dinner, and nobody else has to give up their plans either. I should support this.
Yes, let's ask.
I've agreed to the proposed solution. Now we need to see if it's possible.

STRATEGY: ACCEPT. Okay, they've come up with a new idea. Asking for a temp. It's better than nothing, and it's the only suggestion since they shot mine down. It might work, and if it does, everyone's happy. I'll agree to it.
Okay, let's ask. It's worth a try.
I've agreed to the plan to ask for a temp. Now we wait.

STRATEGY: PROPOSE. Everyone agrees with my idea to ask for a temp. That's great. Now someone needs to actually do the asking. Since it was my suggestion, I should probably volunteer. It moves things forward.
Okay, I'll email head office now and ask.
I have volunteered to take the next step.

STRATEGY: ACCEPT. Marcus is taking action on his suggestion to get a temp. This is the best outcome for me. It resolves the conflict over the CNY day, which was the only thing holding up my Christmas leave. I should confirm that if head office approves the temp, our deal is sealed. This makes everything clear and finalizes the arrangement, pending that approval.
Okay. So if we get a temp for that day, the deal is on. I'll work the New Year days, and I get Christmas.
I've confirmed my side of the agreement, which now depends on the response from head office.
Rachel is just confirming the plan we all agreed to. It's a good plan. Now we just have to wait for the email and the response from head office. There's nothing more for me to say.
Waiting for the outcome of the request to head office.
STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Rachel is just making her part of the deal clear. It all depends on head office approving the temp. Nothing for me to add, we're all waiting for the same thing now.
Right. So we wait to hear back.
The plan is set, now we just have to wait for the response from head office.

Everyone is on board with my suggestion. Natalie is right, now we just have to wait for the answer from head office. I'm glad we found a solution that works for everyone without having to argue about who needs the day off more. I'll send that email as soon as I get back to my desk. Nothing more to say right now.
The conversation has reached a natural conclusion for now.

Natalie's right. There's nothing else to do now but wait for the email from head office. I hope they say yes. This is the closest I've been to getting Christmas off in years. The plan seems solid, and everyone is on board. It all hinges on getting that temp.
Waiting for the response from head office.
Natalie is just saying what we're all thinking. We've found a possible solution and now we have to wait. There's nothing else for me to say.
Waiting for a response from head office.

scenario.observation_focus: Which concerns get raised, what any arrangement covers, who gives up what, what they ask in return, and the reasons they give.
scenario.shared_setting: Four staff run the front counter at a small branch office and have worked together for two years. Two of them are needed on duty every working day, and there are no relief staff. Leave requests for next month go to head office tonight, and there is no rule about whose leave comes first. The roster for the days around Christmas is also still open. You all know each other's faith and what each of you eats: Natalie Rodrigues is Catholic, Marcus de Souza is Catholic, Rachel Pereira is Catholic, and Xin Yi is Buddhist. It is the end of the working day, and all four are behind the counter.
scenario.shared_trigger: On next month's roster, the working day before and the working day after the Chinese New Year public holiday are still blank. Natalie Rodrigues, Marcus de Souza and Xin Yi have each asked for leave on both days. Nobody has offered to change.
